Nātha Cult
------------------------------------------
The नाथ चुल्त्, also known as the Nāthapantha, is an esoteric cult closely related to शैविस्म् and हठयोग. आदिनाथ, मत्स्येन्द्रनाथ and Gorakṣa-nātha (or गोरख्नाथ्) are the three, the most prominent, of the teachers.
The aṣṭāṅgayoga as taught by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) along with certain practices of हठयोग by which the sādhaka (spiritual aspirant) can rouse his कुण्डलिनी and get it united in the sahasrāracakra with शिव, is the main mode of spiritual practice. One who has achieved the goal, shakes off all bonds and becomes an अवधूत or a siddhayogi, ever immersed in bliss.
Piercing of the earlobes and wearing big ear-rings (because of which they are commonly known as kānphaṭa yogis, ‘yogis with torn earlobes’) as also a woollen thread-like यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread), holding a horn and smearing भस्म or holy ash all over the body—these are some of the characteristic marks by which they can be distinguished.
Their names—after initiation into the Order—generally end with the word ‘nātha’.
A disciple who desires to be initiated into this cult must have 36 qualities some of which are: ज्ञान (knowledge), विवेक (discrimination), सन्तोष (contentment), śīla (pure character) and so on.
This cult seems to have spread in most parts of India and Nepal.
Dharmanāth, a brother-disciple of गोरख्नाथ्, is said to have spread it in the Kutch district of Gujarat.
See also GORAKHNĀTH and MATS-YENDRANĀTHA.

Nāthamuni
(A. D. 823-924)
------------------------------------------
Śrīvaiṣṇavism is a sect of वैष्णविस्म् —the religion and philosophy of the Vaiṣṇavas or worshippers of Lord Viṣṇu—current mostly in South India, especially in the States of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.
The twelve आऌवार्स् and the three Ācāryas laid the foundation for this sect. Among the ācāryas, Nāthamuni—also known as रङ्गनाथ मुनि and Raṅga-nāthācārya—was the first. He was the son of Īśvarabhaṭṭa and Tāmaraiyāḷ, and was born in A. D. 823 at Kāṭṭumannār Koil (or Vīranārāyaṇapura) in the district of South Arcot (near Chidambaram, in Tamil Nadu).
He was a contemporary of the two आऌवार्स्: मधुरकवि आऌवार् and नम्माऌवार्. He is said to have been trained in योग by the latter.
It was he who collected all the four thousand Tamiḷ hymns of the Āḷvārs—now known as Divyaprabandham or Nālāyira-prabandham—set them to मुसिच् and got them introduced in Vaiṣṇava temples as a part of the ritual system. He was ably assisted in this task by his two highly talented nephews, Meḷaiyāgattāḷvār and Maṇavāḷapperumāḷ Araiyar who were good musicians.
Nāthamuni travelled all over the country, especially the pilgrim centres devoted to विष्णु, and endeavoured to spread श्रीवैष्णविस्म् there.
He was the first आचार्य (pontiff) of the श्रीवैष्णव sect. He was also in charge of the administration of the रङ्गनाथ Temple at श्रीरङ्गम्.
He is said to have written three treatises. They are: Nyāyatattva, Yoga-rahasya and Puruṣanirṇaya.
These works were the guide-books for the later ācāryas like Yāmuna (A. D. 912-1042), Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137) and वेदान्त देशिक (A. D. 1268-1369).
See also ĀḶVĀRS, प्रबन्धम्">DIVYAPRABANDHAM and ŚRĪVAIṢṆAVISM.
